title: The Components of Direct Instruction i.org/research/journal-of-di/volume-3-no-2-summer-2003/449-the-components-of-direct-instruction/file
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), October 21, 2025 — original paper: https://www.nifd
summary: Barton's page draws on Watkins and Slocum's review of Direct Instruction's three components — program design, organization of instruction, and student-teacher interaction techniques — and connects them to the results of Project Follow Through, the largest educational experiment in history. In that study, DI was the only model to produce significant positive outcomes on basic skills, cognitive-conceptual measures, and affective measures, raising disadvantaged students' achievement to national norms. The summary works through practical mechanics: flexible skill-based grouping, brisk but think-time-respecting pacing, scripted presentations delivered with performance-level skill, and a model-test-retest correction procedure used the moment an error appears. It stresses that mastery should be judged by the group's lowest performer, not the average, and that placement and pacing decisions should be driven by ongoing data rather than teacher hunches. The piece also pushes back on the common misconception that DI is rote learning by design, arguing its real focus is generalizable strategies and higher-order thinking.
points: In Project Follow Through, Direct Instruction was the only model of dozens tested to show significant positive outcomes on basic skills, cognitive-conceptual, and affective measures with nearly 100,000 disadvantaged children.
Mastery should be judged by the performance of the lowest-achieving student in the group, not the class average, so that no one is quietly left behind.
Corrections follow a strict model-test-retest procedure delivered to the whole group during unison responses, never singling out an individual student.
Grouping should be based on mastery of specific skills, not general ability labels, and should be adjusted continuously as performance data comes in.
quotes: The provided text offers a comprehensive overview of Direct Instruction (DI), an educational approach designed to teach subject matter efficiently to ensure all students master the material.

Direct Instruction was the only model in Project Follow Through to show significant positive outcomes on basic skills, cognitive-conceptual, and affective measures, raising disadvantaged students' achievement to national norms.
Grouping is based on mastery of specific skills needed for the program, not general characteristics like intelligence, which is incompatible with DI.
Teachers must notice every error and provide immediate, explicit, and direct corrections. The basic procedure involves model-test-retest.
As can be seen, the Direct Instruction model was the only model to demonstrate significant positive outcomes on basic skills measures, cognitive–conceptual measures, and affective measures.
